chunks: "A decoupling or bypass capacitor is a small capacitor placed right at an IC's supply pin to ground. It does two things.
It supplies the fast bursts of current the IC needs when its transistors switch, because the regulator and the traces back to it have too much inductance to respond in nanoseconds.
And it shunts high-frequency noise on the supply to ground so it doesn't reach the chip, and so the chip's own switching noise doesn't get out onto the rail.
Typically that's a 100 nanofarad ceramic per supply pin, sometimes with a 10 or 1 nanofarad.
A bulk capacitor is a much larger one, tens to hundreds of microfarads, often electrolytic, tantalum, polymer or a bank of ceramics, placed near where power enters the board or the load.
It handles low-frequency demand: slower load steps, in the microsecond to millisecond range, the time it takes the regulator's control loop to respond, and it holds up the rail through that gap.
The difference is the frequency band, and the physical size and parasitics.
Big capacitors have high ESL, so they stop being capacitors at maybe a megahertz; small ceramics with low ESL work up to tens of MHz.
So you need both, plus intermediate values, and you place them in order, with the smallest closest to the pin.
I'd size them from a target impedance: the allowed voltage ripple divided by the transient current, and then check the impedance curve for anti-resonance peaks."
